A piece of woodland, the usufruct of which his family had enjoyed for generations, was suddenly claimed by the Patteel of the village, who sent six workmen to fetch the wood. The facts of the case can brietly be summarised as under : - : A member of this Association, Mr. Chaturbhoj Sheevji, who is also the Chairman, had sold in Samvat year 1970 certain goods to two of the members, Mr. Ramdas Girdhar and Mr. Premchand Vrajlal. According to the rules of the Association the value of the goods was debited to the buyers' account either on date of delivery or, when no delivery was taken within eight days from date of sale, on the eighth day. The tules of the Association provide that payment shall be made on the 17th day for retail' goods and on the 11th day for wholesale goods, from the date the goods are debited, 'in default of which the buyer shall pay interest at nine per cent.

As is customary in the trade the accounts were made up with compound interest, as nothing contrary to this procedure is mentioned in the rules of the Association. To this the abovementioned buyers took objection, contending that the sellers were not entitled to compound interest as no mention is made to that effect in the rules, and also because the entry of interest was not made in the books of the seller at the end of the year. The dispute was ultimately referred to their Association and the Committee decided that the seller was entitled to charge compound interest, This judgment caused an uproar amongst petty dealers who were unwilling to bear the interest on the interest, and a. requisition signed by 80 members was sent to the Secretaries requesting thém to call a general meeting of their Association to reconsider the resolution of the Committee.

Aiter dealing with the past and present history of Ireland, and avowing himself an extreme Home Ruler, Mr. Burrows went on to djscuss the question pf India, applying to it the same fundamental principles which he had laid down with respect to Treland. The Indian problem was, he said, an enormous and a difficult one and could not be neglected, or else it might solve itself in a way unpleasant to England. He personally did not helieve that, because of India's contributions in men and money to the war, the British Government would as a matter of course give India much of what she desired in the way of self-government. There might perhaps be an extension of provincial autonomy, a small widening ef Indian representation on the legislative councils and the Viceroy's Council, but England would still retain the dominating upper hand.

Education must be liberally and impartially extended in accordance with the best Indian ideas, and the fixed idea of race-superiority must be given up. These were matters for England.
